# Brief: Monster Hotel (`monster-hotel`)

Read `docs/build/CLOUD.md` first. This brief is the whole contract for your game; the guide it points to holds the rules.

## The game

- Key: `monster-hotel`. Name: Monster Hotel. Age band: 9 to 12. Emoji: 🏨.
- Generator: `npm run new:game -- monster-hotel "Monster Hotel" 9-12 🏨`
- Branch: `lane/monster-hotel`. Base branch: `feat/learning-games-build`. Base commit: the one your starting message names.
- Subject and the skill that is the verb: Feelings: taking another's point of view, and settling wants that conflict.
- Suggested renderer: canvas 2D ("Canvas or three.js" in the guide decides what follows from it). Say in the sheet if you choose otherwise, and why.
- It comes from no demo: it is a new design.

## The idea

Monster guests with wants that collide: one plays the tuba at night and the neighbour sleeps by day; one wants the heating up and one wants snow. The child gives out rooms and arranges things, and can look at the hotel from any guest's place to see what that guest sees and minds. Any arrangement that leaves everyone content stands, and there are several. Deadpan and a little absurd; nothing babyish.

The owner's bar for every game: lively and funny, never slow or quiet; animated, cute and warm; deep enough to come back to for weeks through combinations and characters; with no score, coin, streak, reward, praise or timer that pushes. Short animated scenes are welcome where the guide allows them.

### Notes
- Standing decides the wording of the claim. In California, taking another's point of view and fairness rest only on voluntary guidance (say "voluntary guidance", never "standard"), in bands the document ties to no grades. Adopted records on conflict exist for grade 4 and grade 6 only; grade 5 health has no social or emotional area, so nothing adopted is named for ages 10 to 11. In the Netherlands every fase record is guidance (there is no social-emotional line for fase 2 or 3; these goals stand in the line on oneself and the other). The end-of-primary goals in force (35 and 37, legal-core-goal, regime 2006, confirmed) name neither point of view nor conflict; the two records that do are drafts, cited as "draft core goal, not in force".
- Difference at 9 to 10: California grade 4 asks for practising a settlement with other people; the Dutch fase 2 records ask for discussing where a conflict comes from and for taking others into account (also ojw/ja/3/08/fase2, `edu.nl.fase-2.practical-life-feelings.objective.5a82ef6a-dd10-4043-9079-4e3496f50b4b`, confirmed: putting into words how a simple conflict arose and which solutions are possible). "Solutions that suit every party" is fase 3 (10 to 12). Follow nl for the verb of play at 9 to 10 (see what each side wants and feels, then name possible solutions). Reason: settling the quarrels of monsters on a screen is not practice with other people, which the Limits of 4.4.2.S asks for; the game is "designed from" 4.4.2.S and 6.4.4.M and never says the child has practised them.
- The child here settles a conflict between others. The Dutch fase 3 record leaves open whether the child is a party; the two adopted California records read as the child's own conflicts; the voluntary records 5.F.2 and 4.E.3 fit a go-between best.
- Fairness is named by no adopted standard and no law in force. It rests on voluntary us-ca 5.F.2 (best for all it touches) and 5.B.2 (`edu.us-ca.cross-grade.practical-life-feelings.objective.late-elementary-5-b-2`, voluntary-guidance, confirmed: expects fair treatment from adults and children), on the Dutch fase 3 "suits every party" and on draft 20 A d. No record defines fair as equal shares. Narrow "fairness" to "a solution every side can accept".
- 4.4.2.S stands in a health area the pack's map marks as sensitive; this record itself is about disagreements, and the neighbouring records on violence and bullying are not needed.
- No score or verdict on the child's empathy, on the kid side or in a grown-up corner. Every record named is `confirmed`; the two drafts are confirmed as records and are not law.

## This run

This run covers the design and the rules. The template you start from is its second version, proven by a three.js game; the canvas pilot (Monster Pizza) is proving it for a canvas game first, so you do not build your toy yet.

1. The steps under "Getting the code" in the cloud page.
2. The design sheet, pushed with `Open: sheet ready for check, round 1`.
3. The look spike for your first reserved look: the game's real scene in the style, at the quality bar, shown by the Mount at load with a fixed seed and with nothing playable behind it.
4. The rules as pure modules with tests beside them (no renderer, no DOM), in new files of your own, leaving the copied template files as they are wherever you can: the model of the world, the object-by-action grid, the errors as consequences, the characters' tastes, the designed order with its position ids in `config.ts`, the saved state with its defensive `deserialize`, and the size test. The guide lets a remote builder write rules while the check of its sheet runs, at its own risk: record in the status block the sheet commit they were written against.
5. Stop there: write the status block, push, and report. Your next message brings the checker's report on your sheet and the commit that holds what the canvas pilot changed in the template.

Numerals and mathematics signs are allowed in your band, and the module that draws them, `symbols.ts`, is being proven by one game first (Fruit Slicer). In this run, design where each numeral lies in the sheet and in the pure rules, and draw none yet: your next message names the commit that holds the module to start from.
